title: Chapter 46
paragraphs: Although Marianne's illness was weakening by nature, it had not lasted long enough to make her recovery slow. Helped by youth, natural strength, and her mother's presence, she improved steadily. Within four days of Mrs. Dashwood's arrival, she could move into Mrs. Palmer's dressing room. There, at Marianne's express request, Colonel Brandon was invited to visit. She was eager to thank him for bringing her mother.

His emotion on entering, seeing her changed appearance, and taking the pale hand she immediately offered seemed to Elinor to arise from more than his love for Marianne or his knowledge that others knew of it. In his melancholy eyes and changing colour as he looked at her, Elinor soon recognised the probable return of many painful memories. The resemblance between Marianne and Eliza, which he had already acknowledged, was now strengthened by her hollow eyes, sickly skin, reclining weakness, and warm gratitude for an exceptional obligation.

Mrs. Dashwood watched no less closely than her daughter. But her mind was influenced quite differently, and her observations produced quite different results. She saw nothing in the Colonel's behaviour beyond the simplest, most obvious feelings. In Marianne's words and actions, meanwhile, she persuaded herself that something beyond gratitude was already beginning.

After another day or two, with Marianne visibly stronger every twelve hours, Mrs. Dashwood began to speak of returning to Barton, urged equally by her own wishes and her daughter's. The plans of their two friends depended on _hers_. Mrs. Jennings could not leave Cleveland while the Dashwoods stayed. Their united requests soon persuaded Colonel Brandon to regard his own stay as equally fixed, if not equally essential. In return, he and Mrs. Jennings together persuaded Mrs. Dashwood to use his carriage for the journey home, for the greater comfort of her recovering child. The Colonel gladly agreed to collect it by visiting the cottage in a few weeks. This invitation came jointly from Mrs. Dashwood and Mrs. Jennings, whose active kindness made her generous and hospitable on other people's behalf as readily as her own.

The day of parting arrived. Marianne took an unusually attentive, prolonged farewell of Mrs. Jennings, full of earnest gratitude, respect, and good wishes, as though her own heart required it in private acknowledgement of past neglect. She said goodbye to Colonel Brandon with the warmth of a friend. He carefully helped her into the carriage, anxious, it seemed, that she should occupy at least half of it. Mrs. Dashwood and Elinor followed. The others were left to discuss the travellers and feel their own dullness until Mrs. Jennings was called to her chaise. Her maid's gossip must now comfort her for losing her two young companions. Immediately afterwards, Colonel Brandon set out alone for Delaford.

The Dashwoods travelled for two days, and Marianne bore both without serious fatigue. Each watchful companion did everything devoted love and anxious care could suggest to make her comfortable. Both found their reward in her physical ease and calm spirits. Elinor particularly welcomed the latter. She had watched her sister suffer week after week, burdened by a misery she had neither courage to discuss nor strength to hide. Now she saw an apparent peace of mind with a joy nobody else could equally share. If, as she trusted, it came from serious reflection, it must eventually lead to contentment and cheerfulness.

As they approached Barton, however, every field and tree recalled something particular and painful. Marianne grew quiet and thoughtful, turning her face away and gazing intently through the window. Elinor could neither wonder nor blame her. Helping her from the carriage, she saw that Marianne had been crying. The emotion was too natural to inspire anything less tender than pity, and its quietness deserved praise. Everything in her subsequent behaviour suggested a mind awakened to reasonable effort. The moment they entered the sitting room, Marianne looked firmly around, apparently determined to accustom herself at once to every object connected with Willoughby. She spoke little, but every sentence attempted cheerfulness. A sigh sometimes escaped, yet was always followed by a compensating smile. After dinner she tried the piano. The first music she saw, however, was an opera Willoughby had obtained for her, containing some of their favourite duets and bearing her name on the cover in his handwriting. That would not do. Shaking her head, she put it aside. After running her fingers over the keys for a minute, she complained that they were weak and closed the instrument. As she did so, however, she firmly declared that she would practise a great deal in future.

The next morning brought no weakening of these encouraging signs. Rest had strengthened body and mind alike. She looked and spoke with more genuine animation, anticipating Margaret's return and the restoration of their dear family circle. Their shared pursuits and cheerful companionship were, she said, the only happiness worth wishing for.

“When the weather settles and I have my strength back,” she said, “we shall take long walks together every day. We shall go to the farm beside the down and see how the children are getting on, to Sir John's new plantations at Barton Cross, and to Abbeyland. Often we shall visit the old Priory ruins and try to trace the foundations as far as we are told they once extended. I know we shall be happy. I know the summer will pass happily. I intend never to rise later than six, and from then until dinner I shall divide every minute between music and reading. My plan is formed: I mean to undertake serious study. I know our own library too well to use it for anything beyond amusement. But there are many worthwhile books at the Park, and more recent works I know I can borrow from Colonel Brandon. Reading only six hours a day, I shall gain a great deal of the knowledge I now lack within a year.”

Elinor respected a plan arising from such worthy intentions. Still, she smiled to see the same eager imagination which had carried Marianne to extremes of idle listlessness and selfish complaint now introducing excess into a scheme of sensible occupation and virtuous self-control. Her smile became a sigh when she remembered her unfulfilled promise to Willoughby. She feared she must communicate something that might unsettle Marianne again and destroy, at least temporarily, this promising prospect of peaceful activity. Wanting to postpone the painful moment, she decided to wait until her sister's health was stronger. But she made the resolution only to break it.

Marianne had been home two or three days before the weather became fine enough for someone recovering from illness to go out. At last a mild, pleasant morning encouraged both her desire and her mother's confidence. Leaning on Elinor's arm, she was permitted to walk in the lane outside the house for as long as she could without tiredness.

The sisters walked slowly, as Marianne's weakness required in exercise she had not attempted since her illness. They had gone only far enough for a full view of the hill behind the house—that important hill—when Marianne paused, looked towards it, and calmly said,
“There, just there”—she pointed with one hand—“on that jutting mound. That is where I fell, and where I first saw Willoughby.”
Her voice faded on his name, but she soon recovered it and continued.
“I am grateful that I can look at the place with so little pain. Shall we ever speak about it, Elinor?” She hesitated. “Or would it be wrong? I hope I _can_ talk about it now in the way I ought.”
Elinor gently encouraged her to speak freely.

“As for regret,” Marianne said, “I have finished with that, where _he_ is concerned. I do not want to tell you what my feelings for him were, but what they are _now_. If I could be satisfied about one thing, if I could believe that he was not _always_ playing a part, not _always_ deceiving me—and, above all, if I could be certain he was never as _terribly_ wicked as I have sometimes feared since hearing about that unfortunate girl—”
She stopped. Elinor treasured the words with joy and answered,
“If you could be sure of that, you think you would find peace?”

“Yes. My peace depends on it in two ways. It is terrible to suspect someone who meant what _he_ meant to _me_ of such intentions. But what does that make me in my own eyes? In my position, what but shamefully unguarded love could have exposed me to—”
“How, then,” her sister asked, “would you explain his behaviour towards you?”
“I would think him—oh, how gladly I would think him—only changeable, very, very changeable.”
Elinor said nothing further. She was considering whether to begin her story immediately or wait until Marianne was stronger. For several minutes they moved slowly on in silence.
“I do not wish him too much happiness,” Marianne said at last with a sigh, “when I wish his private reflections no more painful than mine. Those will make him suffer enough.”
“Are you comparing your behaviour with his own?”
“No. I compare it with what it should have been. I compare it with your behaviour.”
“Our circumstances have been very different.”

“Less different than our conduct. Dearest Elinor, don't let your kindness defend what I know your judgement must condemn. Illness has made me think. It gave me time and quiet for serious reflection. Long before I was well enough to talk, I could think perfectly clearly. I looked back. From the beginning of our acquaintance with him last autumn, I saw in my own behaviour only a succession of recklessness towards myself and unkindness towards others. I saw that my feelings had prepared my suffering, and that my lack of courage in bearing it had nearly taken me to the grave. I knew I had brought the illness entirely on myself by neglecting my health in ways I understood, even then, to be wrong. If I had died, I would have destroyed myself. I did not know my danger until it had passed. But remembering what those reflections made me feel, I wonder that I recovered. I wonder that my intense desire to live, to have time to make amends to God and to all of you, did not kill me at once. If I had died, what particular misery I would have left you in—my nurse, my friend, my sister! You had seen all the irritable selfishness of those last days, heard every complaint of my heart. How would I have lived in _your_ memory? And our mother! How could you have comforted her? I cannot express how deeply I despised myself. Whenever I looked back, I found some neglected duty or indulged fault. Everyone seemed to have been hurt by me. I had repaid Mrs. Jennings's constant kindness with ungrateful contempt. I had been rude and unjust to the Middletons, Palmers, Steeles, even the most ordinary acquaintances. I had shut my heart against their good qualities and let their very attention irritate me. To John and Fanny—yes, even them, little as they deserve—I had given less than I owed. But you, above everyone, even above our mother, had been wronged. I alone knew your heart and its sorrow. What did that knowledge lead me to? No compassion that helped either of us. Your example was before me, but to what purpose? Did I consider you and your comfort more? Did I imitate your patience, or ease your restrictions by taking any share in the ordinary courtesies and particular expressions of gratitude you had been left to manage alone? No. Knowing you unhappy, I still refused every effort of duty or friendship, just as I had when I thought you content. I scarcely allowed that sorrow existed outside myself. I mourned only _the_ heart that had abandoned and wronged me, leaving you, whom I claimed to love without limit, to suffer on my account.”

Her rapid stream of self-reproach stopped. Eager to comfort her, though too honest to flatter, Elinor immediately offered the praise and support her openness and remorse deserved. Marianne pressed her hand and replied,

“You are very kind. The future must prove me. I have made my plan. If I can keep to it, I shall control my feelings and improve my temper. They will no longer distress others or torment me. From now on I shall live entirely for my family. You, our mother, and Margaret must be my whole world, sharing all my affection between you. I shall never again feel the smallest wish to leave you or my home. If I enter other company, it will only be to show that my spirit is humbled, my heart improved, and that I can perform life's courtesies and smaller duties gently and patiently. As for Willoughby, it would be foolish to say I shall soon forget him, or ever forget him. No change of circumstances or opinion can erase his memory. But I shall govern it and keep it in check through religion, reason, and constant occupation.”
She paused, then added quietly, “If only I could know _his_ heart, everything would be easier.”

Elinor had been weighing the wisdom of telling her story at once for some time, without coming any nearer a decision. Hearing this, she realised that if reflection achieved nothing, determination must do everything. She soon found herself approaching the subject.

She hoped she told it tactfully. She prepared her anxious listener carefully, explained simply and honestly the chief arguments in Willoughby's defence, gave his repentance its due, and softened only his declarations of continuing love. Marianne said nothing. She trembled, stared at the ground, and her lips grew paler than illness had left them. A thousand questions rose in her heart, but she dared ask none. She caught every syllable with breathless eagerness. Without knowing it, she gripped Elinor's hand tightly, while tears covered her cheeks.

Fearing that Marianne was tired, Elinor led her home. Until they reached the cottage door, she spoke only of Willoughby and their conversation. She could easily guess Marianne's curiosity, though no question expressed it, and supplied careful details of every word and look where such detail could safely be given. Once inside, Marianne kissed her gratefully. Through her tears she could just make out two words, “Tell Mama,” before leaving her sister and going slowly upstairs. Elinor would not disturb so reasonable a wish for solitude. Anxiously imagining its effect, and resolved to reopen the subject herself if Marianne did not, she entered the sitting room to carry out her sister's request.
